read.bigIdea: Everyone starts, a few go all the way.
read.where: Our Beer Program has four levels: **Beer Server** for everyone who serves beer, **Beer Specialist** for bartenders, **Advanced Specialist** for beer leads, and **Master of Beer**, by **invitation**: a manager invites the person in People. Cicerone’s outside ladder runs the same way: **Certified Beer Server** (60 questions, **75%** to pass), **Certified Cicerone** (80% overall, 70% on tasting), **Advanced Cicerone** (80%, 75% on tasting), **Master Cicerone**. As the program lead, you decide who’s ready for the next level and **coach** them through it.
read.mixup: Our certificates aren’t Cicerone’s. They prepare people for Cicerone’s exams; only Cicerone awards its titles.

video.title: Happy Staff, Happy Guests: Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for Bars

read.where: A program runs on a written **standard**: one page at the bar and in the walk-in. Put the numbers on it, from the Draught Beer Quality Manual: store **34–38°F**, serve **38–44°F**, pour about **2 oz a second**, a **beer-clean** glass every pour (never refill a used glass), glasses **air-dried**, lines cleaned every **14 days** with the log signed. Add our own: the head we pour, the glass for each beer, who changes kegs. Then **train** it (Levels 1–3), and **check** it with the monthly audit (Lesson 2).
read.mixup: A standard nobody checks is a suggestion. The audit is what makes it a standard.

read.bigIdea: Suppliers can’t give us things of value.
read.where: Michigan’s Liquor Control Code (**MCL 436.1609**) says a brewer, wholesaler or other supplier **shall not aid or assist** a retailer by **gift, loan** of money or property, or any **other valuable thing**, and the retailer **shall not accept** it. The law lists what’s allowed, including **removable tap markers or signs**, table tents, drink menus and **keg couplers lent** to an on-premises retailer. **Beer-branded glassware** is different: a retailer may use it only if it was **bought from a barware retailer**, and keeps the receipts. Work with reps on **freshness, date codes, release dates and staff training**; anything that looks like a freebie, ask the GM first.
read.mixup: A free case of branded pint glasses from the distributor isn’t a nice gesture. In Michigan we buy branded beer glassware from a barware retailer.

video.title: The Hardest Beer Exam In The World: What it takes to be a Master Cicerone

read.where: Cicerone’s top title is **Master Cicerone**. You must have passed the **Advanced Cicerone** and be of legal drinking age. It’s a **two-day** exam with **written** parts (essay questions), **oral** exams by industry experts, and **tasting** assessments covering a broad range of **off-flavors**. You need **85%** to pass. Very few people hold it. This level, Master of Beer, is ours, not Cicerone’s: it covers the running of one restaurant’s program, and the reading behind it is the same, from the Draught Beer Quality Manual to the BJCP guidelines.
read.mixup: Master of Beer isn’t Master Cicerone. Ours is the restaurant’s certificate; Cicerone’s is earned only from Cicerone.

The Master Cicerone count is left out: Cicerone listed 16 at the end of 2017 and the number has grown since; no current official figure was found.

Supplier rules beyond MCL 436.1609 (federal tied-house rules in 27 CFR Part 6, Commission rules and orders) weren’t worked through: GM to check with the Liquor Control Commission before accepting anything from a supplier. Not legal advice.
